text: This capstone works through one realistic, multi-layered slow-instance problem across all three remaining lessons, pulling together everything this course has covered -- slow forms and lists, slow scripts, database performance, instance health, integrations, and incident response -- into a single diagnosis-and-fix exercise, the way a real performance investigation actually unfolds rather than how a single isolated lesson would present it.

Meridian Retail's custom Store Opening Checklist app grew quietly from 50 pilot stores to 500 stores over six months. Nobody treated that growth as a performance event -- it just happened, a few stores a month, with no review of the app's queries, scripts, or scheduled jobs along the way. Now three symptoms have surfaced: a slow list view, approval flows that feel stuck, and a full 40-minute platform-wide slowdown that hit right at 7 AM, exactly when every one of those 500 stores submits its checklist at once.

Reading Instance Health against the store-growth and deployment timelines together tells a story neither one tells alone. Average list load time is climbing, and climbing faster than store count -- a gradual, accelerating trend, not a single cliff-edge regression. No one deployment lines up with the steepest jump, which argues against one bad release and for a design that simply doesn't hold up as volume and concurrent usage grow.

Before touching anything in production, the right move is a short, named hypothesis list, each one tied to a specific chapter's diagnostic skill: a list-view or related-list problem from Chapter 1, a missing index on a frequently-filtered custom field from Chapter 3, an expensive per-record script pattern from Chapter 2, and scheduled-job semaphore contention at peak load from Chapter 4. A six-month, ten-x growth slowdown rarely has just one root cause, and one hypothesis -- the missing index -- could plausibly explain more than one symptom at once, since the same slow query a list view relies on can also be the query a script re-runs inside a loop.

Jumping straight to a fix right now would be a mistake. Chapter 6's incident-response discipline applies just as much to a slow-growing problem as to a live incident: gather evidence and confirm each hypothesis before changing anything in production. Next, Lesson 24 confirms which of these hypotheses are real, using actual diagnostic evidence for each one -- and finds that more than one of them is contributing to the same set of symptoms at the same time.
